courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Projecting Gaussians to splats and sorting them by tile
md: The sort is per tile, by each Gaussian's center depth, not per pixel. Where two large splats interpenetrate, the true order can differ from pixel to pixel, so blending is approximate. The paper notes this error becomes negligible as splats shrink toward pixel size, and lists sudden order switches (popping) as a limitation.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers and epochs: stop reuse while anyone looks
md: "Garbage collection solves ABA" is a common misconception that Michael calls out. GC prevents ABA caused by *reuse*, but if a program moves the same nodes back and forth between two lock-free stacks, a node can leave and return to the same position with perfect GC. Ask whether the algorithm is ABA-safe under GC first; only then do hazard pointers or epochs make it ABA-safe without GC.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Reporting an ablation people can trust
md: Report per-stage deltas with intervals, the paired test and effect size, win/loss counts, interaction cells for stages that depend on each other, and cost, all on one stated harness. A bare column of mean scores invites the wrong conclusion.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Mass assignment and property-level authorization
md: Field lists rot in one direction: new fields. A blocklist that forbids `isAdmin` today silently allows `isOwner` added next quarter. An allowlist forgets a new field by leaving it read-only, which fails safe.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: NTLM: challenge and response, and why the hash is enough
md: NTLM never sends the password, but its proof is computed only from the unsalted NT hash plus a server challenge. So the hash is the password. Move to NTLMv2 only, then to Kerberos, and watch 4776 and the 4624 package name.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: DCSync: asking a domain controller for every password
md: 4662 is only written if Directory Service Access auditing is on **and** the domain object's SACL asks for it. Many domains have neither, and then DCSync leaves no Security log trace at all. Check before you need it.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Why documents and scripts: the chain an analyst unpicks
md: The first file is rarely the payload. Treat a maldoc, script or shortcut as a list of instructions: read every instruction, follow each stage on paper, and collect indicators at every hop, not only at the end.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Unpacking I: what a packed file looks like, using UPX
md: Section names prove nothing. Whoever builds a file chooses them, so UPX0 may hold a different packer's code and a custom packer may name its sections .text. Trust the measurable signals (entropy, sizes, permissions, imports, entry point) and confirm in a debugger.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Information leaks: why modern exploits start by reading
md: Treat any leak of a pointer, canary or uninitialized byte across a trust boundary as a security bug in its own right. In modern exploits the leak is often the second bug that makes the first one usable.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Deconfliction: is this the red team or a real intruder?
md: Deconfliction protects the organisation, not the red team. Every alert goes through normal escalation; the control group answers "ours or not" from precise operator logs; anything that does not match is a real incident; and the red team pauses when a real intruder may be present.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Regulated red teaming: TIBER-EU, DORA and CBEST
md: Regulated schemes formalise everything in this course: intelligence chooses the adversary, a small control team holds the secret and the stop button, flags define success, leg-ups are logged, every action is recorded, and the test ends in a replay and purple teaming rather than a pass mark.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: From one model call to an agent loop
md: A harness is a loop: call the model, run the tool calls it asks for, append the results, repeat until the model returns no tool calls or a budget runs out. Everything else (context management, permissions, traces, evals) is infrastructure around that loop.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: The write path: extract facts, dedupe and resolve conflicts
md: Misconception: conflict resolution is a database problem you can solve with "latest write wins". Whether two facts conflict is a judgment about meaning ("eats fish" vs "vegetarian" share no words), which is why Mem0 asks an LLM. That also means the resolver can be wrong: a sarcastic "oh sure, I love meetings" can delete a real preference.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Why intrinsic self-correction often fails
md: Self-correction works when the feedback carries information the generator did not have: a failing test, a compiler error, a schema violation, a human note. Asking the same model to "check again" adds calls, not information.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Direct and indirect injection, and how jailbreaks differ
md: Hidden does not mean exotic. White text, zero-size fonts, HTML comments, alt text, document metadata and invisible Unicode characters are all ordinary ways text reaches a model without a human noticing. If your extractor keeps it, the model reads it.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: RAG and vector stores: poisoning and permission leaks
md: Filtering after the model answers is too late: the model has already read the forbidden chunk and may paraphrase it. Filter before the chunk enters the context, using the same permissions as the source system, kept in sync when they change.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Stability: formation energy and energy above the convex hull
md: The hull test is a 0 K, zero-pressure, ordered-crystal calculation (the Materials Project docs state the 0 K, 0 atm assumption). It ignores entropy, so it can favor artificially ordered arrangements of similar atoms that would be disordered at real synthesis temperatures. "On the hull" means "thermodynamically plausible in DFT", not "can be made in a lab".

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Detection is a z-test on the green count
md: The normal approximation is optimistic for short texts. For $T = 50$, $\gamma = 0.25$ and 25 green tokens, $z = 4.08$ and the normal tail is $2.2 \times 10^{-5}$, but the exact binomial tail is $1.2 \times 10^{-4}$, about 5.5 times larger. Use the exact binomial when T is small.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Why the mean and standard deviation hide outliers
md: A score is only as good as its model of normal. Mean and standard deviation break under masking; median and MAD fix that for one variable. For data with clusters and local structure you need scores that look at the joint shape of the data, which is what the next lessons build.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Evaluating detectors when 1 percent of points are anomalies
md: Under heavy imbalance, judge detectors by ranking quality where you will act: AP and the PR curve for the whole ranking, precision@k for the review budget. ROC-AUC hides false alarms because it divides them by the huge number of normal points.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: The authorization code flow with PKCE, step by step
md: The code travels through the browser, so assume it can leak. PKCE ties redeeming it to a secret that never left the client that started the flow.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Classic JWT bugs: alg none, RS256 to HS256, kid and jku
md: Every one of these bugs is the same mistake: letting data inside the unverified token decide how the token is verified. The receiver fixes the algorithm, the key set and the audience; the token only gets to say which of the receiver's keys it used.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Design review in the cycle: deciding which changes get a threat model
md: A design review that happens after the code is written is an audit, not a design review. If the triage questionnaire lives in the pull request template instead of the design template, the expensive decisions (which vendor, where the data lives) are already made.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Security champions, bug bounties and disclosure programmes
md: Champions scale security inside; a VDP with safe harbour invites help from outside. Both fail without the basics: someone answers the reports, and fixes have owners and deadlines.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Why a crash needs both undo and redo
md: Steal creates the need for **undo**, no-force creates the need for **redo**. ARIES allows both, so it must do both, using only the log and a little state stored on each page.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Four ways to tell the model which side a text is on
md: All four designs encode the same idea: one shared vector space, two roles. Use the exact pair (prefixes, instructions or input types) that the model was trained with, on the side it was trained for.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Batch jobs, idempotent pipelines and putting it together
md: Order of checks for each call: cache first (free, instant), then dedupe in-flight duplicates, then a concurrency limit and a rate limiter, then the API with bounded jittered retries. Anything that is not latency-sensitive goes to a batch job. Every side effect is keyed so that re-running the job is safe.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Compare-and-swap: write only if nothing changed, else retry
md: CAS turns "read, compute, write" into "read, compute, write *only if what I read is still there*". The retry loop is the general recipe: load, compute from the loaded value, CAS, and on failure recompute from the value CAS returned.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Zero-shot classification with CLAP audio and text embeddings
md: Choosing an approach: use a pretrained tagger's scores directly when AudioSet classes cover your needs; train a small head on frozen embeddings when you have a few hundred labeled clips; fine-tune when you have more data and compute; use CLAP-style zero-shot when labels change often or you have no labeled audio, and expect lower accuracy than a supervised head on the same classes.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Online attacks: brute force, credential stuffing, password spraying
md: Brute force is one account, many passwords. Credential stuffing is many leaked pairs. Spraying is one password, many accounts. MFA and breached-password checks defeat all three; detection needs counts across accounts, not just per account.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Why research needs a loop, not one retrieval
md: A research agent is not a bigger retrieval call. It is a harness loop whose next query depends on what the last read revealed, and whose output is a set of claims each tied to a source.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: On-demand capacity: tokens per minute and the max_tokens trap
md: Set `max_tokens` close to the longest answer you really need. The AWS docs say it directly: if you hit TPM quotas earlier than expected, reduce max_tokens to better approximate your completions. Measure real output lengths from the `OutputTokenCount` metric that Bedrock publishes to CloudWatch, the AWS monitoring service.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Firmware images: layout, signatures and entropy
md: Everything here uses an image we built from our own code. Real vendor firmware is often covered by licence terms, and some contains other parties' secrets; analyse only devices and images you own or are authorised to test, and never download firmware to attack devices you do not control.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Running ternary models fast: I2_S, lookup tables, real numbers
md: Loading the 2B4T checkpoint in Hugging Face `transformers` (the standard Python model library) saves memory but gives no speed or energy gain; the model card says the efficiency needs the dedicated bitnet.cpp kernels.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: B+trees update in place, and random writes pay for it
md: A B+tree's write cost is set by the **page**, not the row: a random small update rewrites a whole page at a random location. Reads are cheap because each key lives in exactly one place.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: The buffer pool: frames, a page table, pins and dirty pages
md: A buffer pool is a write-back page cache owned by the database. On a miss it must evict some *unpinned* page, and write it out first if it is *dirty*. Everything else in this course is about choosing that page well.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Business impact analysis: from processes to tolerable downtime
md: A BIA turns "everything is critical" into an ordered list: for each process, the impact over time, the resources it needs, and its maximum tolerable downtime, decided by the people who own the loss. Everything later (targets, backups, sites, tests) is sized from it.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Restoring at the right size: Atlassian's two-week outage, April 2022
md: Prevent mass deletion at the API (typed IDs, previews, batch caps, second approvers), make deletion reversible for a period (soft delete), and practise restores at the sizes you will really need. Atlassian met its RPO and still took up to 14 days, because its restore procedure did not fit the shape of the loss.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Crisis management: decisions, workarounds and communication
md: Crisis management decides and speaks; recovery teams fix. Keep a decision log, a fixed update rhythm, one authorised voice, contact lists stored outside production, and manual workarounds written down before they are needed.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Entropy patching: spend compute where the next byte is hard
md: Entropy patching spends a global step where the next byte is hard to predict and lets cheap local layers handle predictable runs. The threshold sets the average patch size, and therefore the compute.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Why C memory bugs compile cleanly and ship
md: C's type system cannot express *who owns this block* or *how long this pointer is valid*. Rust's ownership and borrow rules are exactly that missing information, checked at compile time.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Build a safe type on unsafe: a minimal Vec from scratch
md: MyVec is a teaching subset. It rejects zero-sized types, has no insert, remove, iterators or slice access, and does not handle a panic in the middle of an operation. The Rustonomicon's later Vec chapters add each of these, which is a measure of how much care std's Vec holds.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: The working-set staircase and average access time
md: Think in **miss rate**, not hit rate. CMU's point: 99% hits is twice as fast as 97% when misses cost 100 cycles, because the misses dominate the time.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Validating a graph with interventions
md: Graph first, intervention second. The graph proposes which features matter and how; perturbing those features in the real model is what turns a picture into evidence. Expect directional agreement, not exact numbers.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Inverse propensity scoring turns clicks into unbiased labels
md: IPS fixes the examination part of the bias, not click noise. If users sometimes click irrelevant results, those clicks are also upweighted. Joachims et al. show that, as long as relevant results are clicked more often than irrelevant ones, this bias is order preserving: with enough data the best ranking stays the same, but the estimates are no longer exactly relevance.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: When users need HTML: sanitising with DOMPurify
md: Sanitise as the **last step before insertion**, in the context where it will be used. Sanitising on the server and then running the result through an emoji or link replacer in the browser re-opens the TweetDeck kind of bug: new HTML created after the check, never checked.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Zero-shot classification with prompts, probes and robustness
md: Robustness does not survive adapting CLIP to ImageNet. Fitting a logistic-regression classifier on CLIP features with ImageNet labels raised ImageNet accuracy by 9.2% to 85.4%, yet average accuracy across the shifted datasets slightly decreased. Gains on the training distribution and robustness are different things.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: SCARLETEEL 2023: from a Kubernetes pod to the AWS account
md: SCARLETEEL crossed three evidence domains: the container (runtime telemetry), the cloud control plane (CloudTrail) and a second account (its own CloudTrail). Data events were off and some logging was disabled, so the investigators could only say the attacker "went through the buckets", not exactly what they read.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Landing zones: an account layout that contains failure
md: Common mistake: "our security tooling runs in the management account because it can see everything there." That puts your most targeted tools in the one account no SCP protects. Delegate administration to a Security Tooling account and keep the management account for organization tasks only.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Google Cloud in depth: service accounts, actAs and impersonation
md: Google Cloud escalation runs through service accounts: actAs is PassRole and Token Creator is AssumeRole. Remove Editor from default service accounts, grant both roles on individual service accounts only, and never attach a privileged service account to compute that less trusted code can run on.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Instance roles at scale: IMDSv2 everywhere and a data perimeter
md: Roll a perimeter policy out carefully. Because `aws:SourceVpc` exists only for requests through VPC endpoints, any instance role that calls an AWS service over the public internet will start failing. Test in one account first, and check which services each workload calls.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Lloyd's algorithm by hand, and why the seeds decide
md: k-means++ is the only step here with a guarantee. Arthur and Vassilvitskii prove $E[\phi] \le 8(\ln k + 2)\,\phi_{OPT}$ after seeding alone, before a single Lloyd iteration; the iterations can then only lower it. In scikit-learn `init="k-means++"` is the default (a greedy variant that tries several candidates per step), and `n_init="auto"` means 1 run with k-means++ but 10 runs with `init="random"`.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Evaluating a clustering with and without labels
md: Stability rewards a repeatable answer, not a correct one. With enough restarts k-means finds the k = 2 global optimum every time, so it is perfectly stable, and that optimum is the one that scores ARI 0.41 against the truth. Instability is a useful alarm; stability is not a certificate. Report it next to coverage and, where you have them, labels.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: What -O0, -O2 and -O3 actually switch on
md: An -O level is a bundle of passes. -O0 keeps every variable in memory for debuggability; -O2 is the standard speed level; -O3, -Os, -Og and -Ofast each trade something (size, speed, debuggability, strictness) for something else.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: LTO and ThinLTO: optimizing across source files
md: LTO can expose latent bugs. Code with undefined behavior, or with mismatched declarations of the same function in different files, may have "worked" only because the optimizer could not see across files. When LTO breaks a program, suspect the program first; lesson 5 shows how optimizers exploit UB.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: The observe-act loop: screenshots in, mouse and keyboard out
md: Misconception: the model "sees" the screen continuously. It sees only the screenshots you return, at the moments you return them. If a dialog pops up after your capture, the model does not know about it until the next screenshot.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: How loom takes over the scheduler and walks every schedule
md: Every source of non-determinism must come from loom: no real time, randomness or I/O inside `loom::model`. Determinism is what lets loom replay a schedule and flip one choice at a time.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: What a consistency model promises, and why replicas break it
md: Model A is **stronger** than model B when every history A allows is also allowed by B (A is a subset of B). Stronger models rule out more surprising results, and usually cost more coordination, latency or availability.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Hot keys: perfect key balance, unbalanced traffic
md: Consistent hashing balances keys. Hot keys need a different tool: copies (replication, client caches) for read-hot keys, splitting for write-hot keys, and miss coalescing for keys that expire under load.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Backtracking search with forward checking and MRV
md: Choose the **variable** that is most likely to fail, and the **value** that is most likely to succeed. Every variable must be assigned eventually, so failing early on the hardest one costs nothing and prunes the most. But only one solution is needed, so values should keep the most options open.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: What ships in an image: base images, distroless and scanning
md: Misconception: "we scan, so our images are safe". A scanner only knows published vulnerabilities in recognised packages. It does not find your own code's bugs, a backdoored but unlisted dependency, or a secret left in a layer unless a secret scanner runs too.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: RBAC: roles, bindings and the permissions that escalate
md: Misconception: "they can only create pods, not read Secrets". Pod creation lets them mount any Secret in the namespace into a pod they control and read it from inside. Treat create-pods as read-all-secrets for that namespace, unless admission policy restricts what pods may mount.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Secrets: base64 is not encryption
md: Misconception: "our Secrets are encrypted because they look scrambled in kubectl". That is base64. Check whether the API server has --encryption-provider-config at all, and whether identity is first; the docs list both as signs that encryption at rest is not enabled.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: What an image actually is: layers, unions and digests
md: An image is an ordered list of content-addressed changesets plus a config. Everything else follows from that one sentence: identical layers are stored and transferred once, a deletion only adds a marker, and changing any layer invalidates every layer after it. Order your build steps from least to most frequently changing.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown
md: References point at a response, not at the conversation. Store the ordered ids you displayed, with a version, and resolve ordinals, attributes and *those* against that stored list.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: CoT monitors, and what training against them does
md: Misconception: "the monitor flags less often after training, so the model behaves better." A falling flag rate is what both genuine improvement and obfuscation look like. Without an independent ground-truth check of the behavior, you cannot tell them apart.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Packing the pair: special tokens, segments and the 512-token limit
md: A larger max_length is not free and not always possible. Position embeddings fix the hard limit at training time (512 for BERT), and compute per pair grows with sequence length. For long documents, chunk and take the max (or another aggregate) instead of hoping truncation keeps the right part.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Encoding, hashing and encryption are three different things
md: A hash of a short or guessable value is not secret. There are only 10,000 four-digit PINs; hashing all of them takes a fraction of a second, so a stored SHA-256 of a PIN is as good as the PIN. Lesson 11 covers how passwords must be stored instead.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: RSA with tiny numbers: encryption, signing and padding
md: If you ever write pow(m, e, n) in production code you have built textbook RSA. Call a library's OAEP or PSS function, or better, avoid RSA encryption entirely and use an elliptic-curve key exchange plus an AEAD.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Signature nonces: reuse, weak randomness and deterministic signing
md: Two identical signatures of the same message are harmless with RFC 6979. The alarm is the same r value on two different messages under one key: that means k repeated, and the private key must be considered public.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Why a fast GEMM is a hierarchy of tiles
md: Intensity per tile is not the whole story. Two CTAs that share a row of tiles both read the same slice of A, and the L2 cache may serve the second read. CUTLASS's threadblock rasterization (swizzling the CTA launch order: remapping launch indices to tile coordinates so that CTAs running at the same time cover a compact patch of tiles rather than one long row) exists to make that L2 reuse more likely.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: The CUTLASS 3.x API, epilogues and tuning tradeoffs
md: A tile that maximizes arithmetic intensity can still lose: it may leave a tail wave, spill registers, or leave too little shared memory for stages. Measure with the CUTLASS profiler across candidate configurations rather than trusting one formula.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Three questions before you touch a system: law, permission, ethics
md: "It was public, so it was allowed" is the most common mistake. The ACM Code of Ethics says it directly: "A system being publicly accessible is not sufficient grounds on its own to imply authorization." Lesson 4 shows the opposite mistake too: officials calling ordinary viewing of a public page a crime.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The UK Computer Misuse Act, section by section
md: CMA: s1 knowingly unauthorised access attempt (2 years); s2 with intent to commit a further offence (5); s3 unauthorised impairment (10); s3ZA serious damage (14 or life); s3A tools for those offences (2). Authorisation must come from someone entitled to control that kind of access.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Export controls: Wassenaar and 'intrusion software'
md: Wassenaar (2013, amended 2017) controls intrusion software platforms and development technology, with carve-outs for vulnerability disclosure and incident response. The US implements it through BIS's 2021 rule and License Exception ACE; destination, end user and intended unauthorised use decide when a licence is needed.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Cover-ups and whistleblowing: Uber's CSO and Twitter's security lead
md: When the problem is your own organisation: record the facts, escalate internally to the top, take legal advice, and use lawful external channels (regulators, law enforcement) if ignored. Never relabel a breach, pay for silence, or mislead an investigator.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Fitting a mixing law: RegMix, data mixing laws, judging a mixture
md: Regression methods learn mixture to loss from many cheap runs and search the fit. They work when the fitted function has the right shape and accurate parameters: a linear fit picks a corner, and mis-set laws can lose to uniform weights. Always compare against stratified sampling, and judge data choices with small models scored on continuous metrics.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Counting cache lines: the traffic model and the padding bonus
md: Traffic ratio for a streaming loop is $S/k$: record size over bytes touched. For random access to whole records, the ratio flips against SoA by up to the number of fields.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Keep less: minimisation, retention schedules and legal holds
md: Deleting the primary copy is not deletion. Exports, tickets, caches, logs and backups each need their own retention, and backups usually expire last. Lesson 13 shows a way to make old backups unreadable all at once: encrypt them and destroy the key.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Where DLP acts: endpoints, email, web and cloud
md: Every exception is a hole. Allowlisting a whole team, a whole domain or a whole application because one rule was noisy removes protection from every future leak through that path. Fix the detector, then make narrow, reviewed exceptions with an expiry date.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Why distributed bugs refuse to reproduce
md: DST makes a run a pure function of (code, seed). Faults can then be as aggressive and random as you like, because any failure they provoke can be replayed exactly by re-running one seed.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: CircleCI 2023: when the platform holding your secrets is breached
md: Encryption at rest did not save the secrets, because a running service must decrypt them to use them, and the attacker read the keys from a running process. The only secret a breached CI vendor cannot leak is one it never stored.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Sampling: predict every mask, keep the confident, remask the rest
md: A sampling step is: one forward pass over the whole sequence, a guess at every masked slot, then keep the k most confident guesses and remask the rest. The schedule fixes k per step; the confidence ranking decides the order.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Why prefill stalls decode on a shared GPU
md: Prefill is compute-bound and sets TTFT; decode is memory-bound and sets TPOT. Putting both in one batch makes each phase pay for the other.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: From sectors to partitions to image files
md: Do not stop at the partitions. NIST SP 800-86 counts *free space* (areas not allocated to any partition, including whole deleted volumes) as a place where data may remain. Our lab disk already has 2,047 sectors before the first partition that no file system owns.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Anti-forensics from the defender's side: what each trick leaves
md: The cleanup is evidence too. A 1102 event, a reset journal or deleted shadow copies at 14:35 tell you someone with administrator rights was covering tracks then, which often dates the intrusion better than anything they deleted.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
md: DPO is not "RLHF without a reward". It fits the same Bradley-Terry reward model, just parameterized through the policy. It also inherits the KL objective's $\beta$. What it removes is the separate reward network and on-policy sampling during training.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases
md: Until phase 4, at least one store is complete and current, and the other one is being kept in step with it. That is what makes every earlier step reversible. Plan each phase so it can be rolled out gradually (by percentage of objects or code paths) and rolled back with a flag.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Flipping writes, cutting over and deleting the old path
md: Move one thing at a time, keep one store complete until the very end, and measure agreement continuously. The deletion in phase 4 is the only step that should be hard to undo.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Affine quantization: storing reals as int8 plus a scale
md: Misconception: int8 means the model can only represent values between -128 and 127. The integers are codes; the scale maps them to any real range. What int8 limits is the number of distinct levels (256) inside that range, so the range you pick matters more than the bit width alone.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Ivanti Connect Secure, 2024: chained zero-days and a fooled checker
md: A clean integrity check is evidence, not proof. If an attacker reached root, the checker ran on a system the attacker controls. Trust measurements taken from outside the device, and rebuild when root was possible.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Overthinking: 901 tokens to say 2 + 3 = 5
md: Efficient reasoning asks a different question from test-time scaling. Not 'does more thinking help?' but 'how few thinking tokens reach the same accuracy on this particular problem?'

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Underthinking and early exit: stopping at the right moment
md: Long output does not tell you which failure you have. Overthinking re-solves an easy problem that was already right; underthinking abandons a promising approach on a hard one. The fixes differ: stop earlier in the first case, stay longer on each idea in the second.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: ETW: providers, sessions and consumers
md: ETW is plumbing: providers emit, sessions buffer, consumers read. Most of what Event Viewer, Sysmon and EDR sensors show you rides on it, so an attacker who can switch providers off removes evidence before it is ever written.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Tampering and EDR killers: SUNBURST, BYOVD and AuKill
md: Check your driver-load filter against this case. SwiftOnSecurity's config excludes event 6 for drivers whose signature contains `microsoft`. The driver AuKill abused was signed by Microsoft, so that exclusion would hide its load. Narrow exclusions to drivers you have inventoried, or match against a vulnerable-driver hash list instead of the signer.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Neural NILM, seq2point, and the unseen-house problem
md: Every NILM method injects prior knowledge to resolve an unidentifiable sum. Hart hand-designs it (step signatures), FHMMs encode it as state machines, and neural nets learn it from sub-metered houses. The test that matters is a house the model never saw.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Job titles: taxonomies, seniority and embeddings
md: General-purpose embedding models do not know your abbreviations (`SWE` software engineer, `SDET` software development engineer in test, `RN` registered nurse) and blur words that share context (`sales engineer` vs `software engineer`). Expand abbreviations before embedding, match against many alternate titles rather than one label, and keep an *unknown* outcome instead of forcing the nearest code.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Delegated vs application permissions, and who may consent
md: Delegated means the app is capped by the user; application means the app is capped only by the permission. Restrict who may consent to what, and treat every application permission, especially any with write access, as an admin role held by software.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Devices and the Primary Refresh Token: SSO bound to hardware
md: The PRT is the device's master refresh token. Its strength is the TPM-held session key that signs every use; its weak points are devices without TPMs, attacker-registered devices, and the fact that Conditional Access runs when it is used, not when it is issued.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Taking over admins: help desks, MFA resets and rogue federation
md: Help-desk takeovers turn a phone call into admin credentials, and admin credentials into persistence (federated domains, app secrets, devices). Verify callers out of band, keep admin resets in a small privileged role, require phishing-resistant MFA for admins, and alert on any federation change.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
md: Level-triggered asks "is it ready now?" on every wait. Edge-triggered says "it just became ready" once. With ET you own the state: read or write until `EAGAIN`, or remember that the connection is still ready.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Testing many variants: Bonferroni and Holm corrections
md: Count every comparison you make on a query set, including metrics, variants and earlier papers' tests, and correct for the family. Holm is never worse than Bonferroni. Better still, decide the one comparison you will test before you look.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: RELRO, the GOT and FORTIFY_SOURCE
md: RELRO protects a table of pointers by making it read-only after start-up; FORTIFY stops some overflows before they write. Both are cheap, both are build flags, and both should be on: `-Wl,-z,relro,-z,now` and `-D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3` at `-O2`.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: How big is a line, how to find false sharing, who pads
md: Do not pad on a hunch. Padding costs memory and can push other hot data out of cache, which is why Drepper calls padding every variable unacceptable. Confirm with perf c2c or a before-and-after benchmark that the line is really contended.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: Why a filter breaks greedy search on an HNSW graph
md: Predicate subgraph traversal is the right search strategy (no distance computations wasted on failing nodes), but on a normal HNSW graph the predicate subgraph is sparse and disconnected. ACORN changes how the graph is built, or how neighbors are looked up, so that the predicate subgraph stays connected for any predicate.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Build it: a DeepSeekMoE layer with bias balancing in your GPT
md: Do not read quality conclusions off a run this small. Character-level Shakespeare with a 3.65M-parameter MoE (0.9M active) trains in under an hour per run on a CPU; differences of a few thousandths in validation loss between configurations are within seed noise. What this lab shows reliably is the mechanism: what the router does without balancing, and how each method changes the expert loads.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Tile sizes, GQA head fusion and JIT attention variants
md: FlashInfer = one block-sparse view of every KV layout, attention states merged exactly so work can be split and composed freely, a per-step plan that balances skewed lengths while staying CUDA-graph friendly, and a JIT template so new variants get fused kernels instead of new libraries.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Inductive invariants: from bounded checks to every N
md: An invariant is true in reachable states; an inductive invariant is preserved from *any* state that satisfies it. Model checking finds the first; proofs need the second. Use TLC or Apalache to debug a candidate before you try to prove it. Verus loop invariants, later in the course, carry the same three obligations.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Connecting specs to running code, and the wider tool map
md: Trace validation is testing, not proof: it checks only the runs you logged, and its verdict depends on choosing the right points in the code to log each atomic step. The paper says plainly that it does not provide formal correctness guarantees. Its strength is that it keeps a spec honest at the cost of logging.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Microscaling: one power-of-two scale per 32 values
md: MX formats move fine-grained scaling into hardware: 32 elements share one power-of-two E8M0 scale, applied by the tensor core during the dot product. For 8-bit elements that works well. For 4-bit elements the power-of-two restriction can waste up to a whole binade of FP4's tiny 3.58-binade range.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Scraping and enumeration: Facebook's 530 million phone numbers
md: Any feature that answers "is this identifier on the service, and whose is it" is an enumeration oracle. Cap it, gate it on consent, minimise its answer and watch its traffic.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Fake accounts and Sybil attacks
md: You cannot prove two accounts are two people (Douceur). Make each identity cost something scarce, give new accounts limited power until they earn trust, and look for accounts that act as a group.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Chargebacks, disputes and the true cost of a fraudulent order
md: Chargebacks are the fraud label, and they arrive weeks to months late. A fraudulent order costs goods, shipping and fees, several good orders' worth of margin.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Privacy and fairness of risk models
md: Collect what measurably helps, keep it only as long as needed, and keep it out of other uses. Then measure who your false positives are: an acceptable average can hide an unacceptable burden on one group.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: What vulnerability research is, and the rules you work under
md: Vulnerability research is a loop of find, triage, root-cause, report, fix. Its output is a fixed bug and a regression test, not an exploit, and it starts with permission.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Continuous fuzzing at scale: OSS-Fuzz, ClusterFuzz and Heartbleed
md: Continuous fuzzing turns fuzzing from an event into a property of the project: every commit is fuzzed, every crash is triaged, and fixed reproducers keep guarding the code. If your project parses untrusted input, it belongs in OSS-Fuzz or in ClusterFuzzLite (a lightweight version of ClusterFuzz that runs fuzzers in your CI pipeline).

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Writing the report and coordinating disclosure
md: Report privately with a minimised reproducer, the sanitizer output, a one-sentence root cause and a suggested fix; agree a disclosure date; publish an advisory with versions and credit once users can patch.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Geometric hashing: basis pairs, a hash table, and votes
md: A hard bin boundary is fragile: noise of a few thousandths can push u from 0.249 to 0.251 and the vote goes to the wrong bin. Practical systems search neighboring bins, or, like Astrometry.net, skip fixed bins and do a radius search in continuous code space.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Distance on a sphere, and why degree boxes break
md: Use great-circle distance for the final answer. The sphere itself is a model: the Earth is slightly flattened, and a spherical model gives errors typically up to 0.3%. That is why PostGIS `geography` defaults to `use_spheroid = true`, and Elasticsearch `geo_distance` defaults to `distance_type: arc` (the faster `plane` is documented as inaccurate over long distances and near the poles).

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Batching: why 32 launches lose to one
md: The per-image resize kernel does 0.44 microseconds of memory work and carries 0.9 to 6.7 microseconds of launch overhead. The GPU is idle or draining for most of the wall clock, and no kernel tuning can recover it. The fix is one launch that covers the whole batch.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Expandable segments: growing one segment with virtual memory
md: Fixed segments freeze their size at cudaMalloc time, so shapes that drift leave slivers. Expandable segments separate virtual addresses from physical memory (reserve once, map chunks as needed), so the segment grows contiguously instead.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Shared memory banks and bank conflicts
md: Bank = word index mod 32. Different words in one bank serialize; the same word broadcasts. For column access to a 2D tile, make the row width odd.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: The SOL gap: ranking many kernels by what they can return
md: SOL percentages are not the score you optimize. The triage guide is blunt about it: validate every change against absolute kernel duration, because SOL percentages can drop while the kernel gets faster, for example when you reduce the total work. Duration is the ground truth, not SOL percent.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Why chunk retrieval cannot answer 'what are the main themes?'
md: GraphRAG moves work from query time to indexing time. It pays many LLM calls up front to turn the corpus into a graph and a set of pre-written community summaries, so that global questions can be answered by reading summaries instead of sampling chunks.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Lighter graph RAG: FastGraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG
md: Failure modes to watch in any LLM-built graph: missed entities in large chunks, duplicate nodes from name variants, hallucinated relationships stated with confidence, and summaries that drop the specific quotes users need. Every later stage inherits these errors, and global answers rarely show the raw evidence.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-R1-Zero and R1: RLVR with GRPO at scale
md: "The model discovered reasoning on its own" is an overstatement. Liu et al. (2025, the Dr. GRPO paper you will meet in lesson 7) found that DeepSeek-V3-Base already shows aha-moment style self-reflection before any RL, and the R1 authors themselves say the vivid first-person reasoning style reflects engineered heuristics in the cold-start data. RL amplified behaviors already present in the base model.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Why a flame graph shows where time goes but not why
md: Time profiles answer *where*. Counters answer *why*: low IPC plus many cache misses points at memory, many branch misses points at prediction, high IPC with lots of instructions points at doing too much work.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Power, EM, sound and faults: physical side channels
md: Physical side channels need the attacker close to the device, but that is exactly the threat model of smart cards, phones, payment terminals, hardware wallets and secure enclaves. Hertzbleed shows the line between physical and remote is not fixed: when power controls frequency, power becomes timing.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: What a desync enables, and what defenders see
md: Desync detection is a comparison problem. Log a connection or request identifier at both the front end and the back end, and alert when the request counts or request lines for the same connection differ.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: Detecting, responding, and practising safely
md: Desync and cache attacks are the same lesson twice: when two components interpret one message differently, an attacker chooses the difference. Remove ambiguity (HTTP/2 upstream, strict parsing, origin-declared caching), detect disagreement by comparing tiers, and clean up stored state after every fix.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Choosing, verifying and debugging huge pages in production
md: Huge pages are a trade: TLB reach and shorter walks against contiguity, alignment and memory overhead. Use a hugetlbfs pool when you need certainty, THP in madvise mode when the hot regions are known, and check the counters, because both mechanisms fall back silently.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Local, shared and parallel attention, and converting a Transformer
md: Choosing a layout: global attention layers buy exact recall at any distance for a growing KV cache; sliding windows cap the cache and cap exact recall with it; shared attention saves parameters, not cache; parallel heads keep a little attention, and a little KV, in every layer. Across these designs the published choices cluster around a small share of global attention, about 1 layer in 4 to 1 in 8, spread evenly.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: What OT and ICS are, and why they are not just IT
md: A common mistake is to treat a plant like an office network: run an aggressive vulnerability scan, push patches overnight, reboot to clean an infection. NIST warns that indiscriminate use of IT practices in OT 'may cause availability and timing disruptions'. In OT the security team works with control engineers, not around them.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How attacks on physical processes work
md: Three layers stood between the change and an overflow: humans watching the HMI (defeated by the replay), network monitoring (raised an alert at minute 10), and an independent safety system with its own sensor (tripped at minute 26). Design so that the last layer does not share any path with the first two.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Rules and maps: NERC CIP, IEC 62443, NIST, CISA and ATT&CK for ICS
md: Frameworks tell you what good looks like (62443, NIST), what is mandatory in your sector (NERC CIP for the bulk grid), and how attackers behave (ATT&CK for ICS). Use all three, but remember the cases: most real compromises came through remote access, default passwords and flat networks.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: OIDC as the modern alternative: the same job in JSON
md: SAML and OIDC answer the same questions: who issued this, about whom, for which app, for which login, until when, signed with which key. Learn the questions, and either protocol's fields become a checklist.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: The federation defender's checklist, and where to practise
md: Federation turns identity into a few keys and a trust list. Guard those like domain controllers, verify assertions with libraries that use only what was signed, keep sessions short and revocable, and join IdP and app logs so a login that the IdP never issued stands out.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: PAM vaults: check-out, rotation, and the Uber 2022 script
md: A PAM vault turns many secrets into one, rotates them after use, and ideally never shows them to people. That makes the vault and its administrators the most valuable target you own: protect them as the top of the control plane.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
md: Otsu always returns a threshold, even when nothing changed. On a pair with pure noise it will happily split the noise into two classes and flag a large fraction of the image. Check for a clear gap (or a minimum difference between class means) before trusting the mask.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Declaring, severity, the incident commander and the first hour
md: The IC decides and coordinates; they should not also be the person typing commands. When the IC is debugging, nobody is commanding.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Eradication and recovery: rebuild, credentials, krbtgt and backups
md: Replication is not backup. Synchronised copies (domain controllers, mirrored disks, cloud sync) receive the attacker's deletions and encryption as fast as your legitimate changes. Keep at least one copy offline and immutable, and practise restoring it.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Why escaping is fragile
md: Denylist filters ("block quotes, OR, UNION and --") are escaping's weaker cousin. They reject real input such as O'Brien, and they only stop the spellings someone thought of: SQL accepts comments, different case, different whitespace and many equivalent expressions. Lesson 9 shows a real product whose cleaning function was bypassed by finding a path where it was not applied.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Links, drains, timeouts and a CQ that never overflows
md: Size the **CQ** for the maximum number of completions that can be outstanding (including several per request for multishot operations, which post many completions from one request, lesson 5), not the SQ. Use `IORING_SETUP_CQSIZE` with `cq_entries`, and reap promptly.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: ReDoS: a regular expression that blocks every user
md: A backtracking regex is dangerous when one string can be matched in many ways: a quantifier inside a quantifier, alternatives that overlap such as `(a|a)*`, or several `.*` in a row. The slow case is the near miss, so a test with matching strings will never show it. On Node.js the cost is paid by every user of the process.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Finding and catching JavaScript bugs: tools, signals, practice
md: One idea runs through the whole course: in JavaScript the boundaries you assume (an object, a context, a module, a header, a renderer) are usually not security boundaries. Real boundaries are processes, operating system users, origins and authenticated messages. Put untrusted input and untrusted code behind one of those, and check permission where the data is used.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Checking linearizability: searching for a legal order
md: Linearizability checking is a search for one legal order inside the real-time constraints. Its cost is driven by how many operations overlap, so you control it by limiting operations per key and by turning known non-effects (like timed-out reads) into `:fail`.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Measuring, caching and promoting without regressions
md: Three defences, in order: prune what cannot run, search within a budget you chose from a convergence curve, and promote only wins that are larger than the noise. A tuner without the third one is a random walk through your performance history.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Why chains of elementwise ops are memory bound
md: For memory-bound kernels, runtime is roughly bytes moved / bandwidth. Elementwise ops do so little math per byte that the only lever that matters is how many bytes cross the HBM boundary. Fusion cuts bytes, not FLOPs.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: The distillation loss and why it is scaled by T squared
md: Soft gradient = (q - p) / T, which shrinks like 1 over T squared. Multiply the soft loss by T squared so temperature changes what is matched without changing how much it counts.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: When distillation works, when it fails, and what it costs
md: A more accurate teacher is not automatically a better teacher, and a student that improves is not necessarily copying its teacher. Measure student accuracy directly; try a smaller or early-stopped teacher, or a teacher assistant, when the gap is large.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Beyond rounding: pre-RoPE keys, outliers, and FP8 in production
md: Rounding error depends on the range of each group. Pre-RoPE keys, per-channel groups, sparse outliers and an FP16 first token all exist to keep group ranges narrow.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Reload or recompute: bytes versus prefill FLOPs
md: Compare bytes over bandwidth with FLOPs over throughput. Fast tiers (host DRAM, RDMA pools) beat prefill at almost any length; slow tiers only pay off for long prompts, big models, or a GPU that is busy anyway.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Lamport clocks: a counter that respects happened-before
md: Lamport clocks do not detect concurrency. From $L(a) < L(b)$ you may conclude only that b did not happen before a. Any code that treats a larger Lamport timestamp as "definitely caused by" is wrong.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Searching millions of passages: candidates, centroids, PLAID
md: Cheap approximate scores filter, exact scores decide. PLAID is the same funnel as BM25 followed by a cross-encoder, built inside one model: centroid ids are the cheap representation and decompressed vectors are the precise one.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Build Coconut: stage data, loss mask and the multi-pass forward
md: A Coconut training step is n + 1 cached forward passes whose logits are joined into one loss. Gradients flow back through every pass, so time and stored activations both grow with the number of thoughts.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: An index is a model: predicting where a key sits
md: A learned range index is a model of the key CDF plus two stored numbers per model, min_err and max_err. The model makes a guess; the error bounds turn the guess into a guarantee for every stored key.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Why learn sparse vectors instead of dense ones
md: A learned sparse vector is still a bag of weighted terms, so it can live in a normal inverted index. The transformer only decides *which* terms get *how much* weight, including terms absent from the text.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaMART: boosted trees that fit the lambdas
md: LambdaMART = gradient boosted regression trees whose regression targets are the LambdaRank lambdas, recomputed after re-sorting at every round.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Chunkwise DeltaNet derived: WY form and the UT transform by hand
md: The WY form and the UT transform turn C sequential rank-1 updates into one small C x C triangular solve plus matmuls ($KK^\top$, $TK$, $TV$, $WS^\top$, $QK^\top$, $D^\top K$). Only that solve and the hand-off of the state between chunks remain sequential.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Setuid, setgid and sticky: borrowed privilege and its bugs
md: "It is only a local bug" is a dangerous phrase. Local privilege escalation means any foothold, such as a hijacked web application running as `www-data`, becomes root. PwnKit and Dirty COW both needed only an ordinary account.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Reading Linux logs: journald, auth.log, failed logins and sudo
md: Learn the shape of four lines: Failed password, Accepted (password or publickey), sudo COMMAND, and sudo denials. Then look for sequences, not single lines: failures then success from one source, and a fresh login followed by privileged changes.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Measuring a service sandbox with systemd-analyze security
md: Every directive can break something: `MemoryDenyWriteExecute` breaks JIT runtimes, `ProtectProc=invisible` can break tools that inspect other processes, `ProcSubset=pid` is, per the manual, not suitable for most non-trivial programs. Add directives one at a time on a test host and watch the journal for denials.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Falco: turning the system call stream into alerts
md: Falco watches system calls. In April 2025 the security company ARMO showed a proof-of-concept rootkit that does its file and network work through io_uring (lesson 6), and reported Falco's default rules did not see it. Lesson 13 covers what that means for every syscall-based sensor.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Patching a fleet: automatic updates, restarts, reboots and rings
md: "Installed" is the most common false comfort in patch reports. The xz-utils and regreSSHion fixes did nothing for a daemon that kept running the old code; libraries need service restarts and kernels need reboots or livepatches. Report on what is running.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: From labels to leaderboards: do system rankings survive?
md: Label-level agreement can be modest (kappa 0.3 to 0.6) while system-level agreement is high (tau near 0.9), because errors that are not systematic average out over many queries. The reverse also holds: a small systematic bias can flip close systems even when kappa looks fine.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Task-specific eval sets, regression tests and significance
md: Report a gain as an interval, computed by resampling items with both systems paired. If the interval includes zero, say "not distinguishable on this set" and either add items or keep the old version. Check slices as well as the average.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: KV cache accounting: from bytes per token to batch size
md: Capacity in sequences is roughly pool bytes / (bytes per token x tokens per sequence). Every lever (GQA, FP8 KV, more GPUs, smaller weights, shorter contexts, less waste per sequence) moves one of those three terms.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Why asking nicely for JSON is not enough
md: Three different promises are easy to confuse: *parses as JSON*, *matches my schema*, and *is correct*. JSON mode gives the first, schema-constrained output gives the second, and only your own validation and evaluation can check the third.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Evaluating the parser with exact match per field
md: The predictions in this lesson are hand-written to show typical error types. They are not measurements of any model. Use the method, not the numbers.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Prefix caching, truncation and smaller candidate lists
md: Every input saving has a quality price. Truncation can cut the sentence that made a passage relevant. A smaller $k$ means relevant documents retrieved at rank 31 or lower are never reranked. Measure NDCG@10 at each setting on your own queries before shipping the cheaper one.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Evaluating routers: cost-quality curves, PGR, APGR and CPT
md: Read router claims carefully. "2x cheaper at the same quality" depends on the benchmark, the model pair, the quality target and the baseline. RouteLLM's savings are measured against a random router, not against a GPT-4-only deployment, and vary from 1.41x to 3.66x across three benchmarks. Only an evaluation on your own prompts tells you what you will get.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: RANSAC: keeping only matches that agree on one homography
md: RANSAC finds the model that the most matches agree on by fitting minimal random samples. The cost grows as $1/w^s$, so cleaner matches (a good ratio test) and smaller samples make it dramatically cheaper.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Vyukov's bounded MPMC queue: a sequence number per cell
md: Vyukov is explicit: the queue is "not lockfree in the official meaning, just implemented by means of atomic RMW operations w/o mutexes" (RMW is read-modify-write: an instruction such as CAS or fetch-add that reads and writes a location in one indivisible step) and classifies it as having blocking producers and consumers. It is still excellent in practice; just do not cite it as a lock-free progress guarantee.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drift when a release changes the format, and a pipeline that holds
md: The misconception that costs the most: that a template id is a stable name for a logging statement. It is a name for a *cluster*, and clusters split, merge, get wildcarded and get evicted. Anything long-lived (a dashboard, an alert rule, a trained model) must key on persisted template text plus an explicit supersedes relation, not on whatever integer the miner handed out last Tuesday.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: MITRE ATT&CK as a coverage map
md: A green cell is not protection. One rule tagged with a technique usually catches one or two of the many ways to perform it. Count a technique as covered only if a test of a realistic procedure produced an alert (lesson 17), and record which procedures were tested.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Position Interpolation and NTK-aware scaling
md: Do not confuse the two knobs. PI rescales *positions* (every pair by the same $1/s$). NTK-aware changes the *base* (each pair by a different amount). Both leave the model architecture unchanged; only the precomputed cos and sin tables differ.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Does the model use its context? Evaluation
md: Extending RoPE (PI, NTK, YaRN) makes long positions *in distribution*; Ring Attention and context parallelism make long sequences *fit*; neither guarantees the model *uses* the context. Measure effective length with depth-controlled tasks such as RULER.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Build it: loop your GPT with input injection and random depth
md: Everything here is one seed of a 219K-parameter model on a synthetic task. Treat the numbers as a demonstration of the mechanism (more iterations resolve deeper chains, exits track depth, starts are forgotten), not as evidence about which adapter is better at scale.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: LoRA: a frozen weight plus a trainable low-rank update
md: LoRA = frozen W0 + (alpha/r) B A, with B initialized to zero. You train r times (d + k) numbers per adapted matrix, and the model starts exactly at the pretrained one.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Unlearning by replacement: Who's Harry Potter and RMU
md: Replacement methods give the model something specific to do instead: predict generic tokens (WHP) or produce scrambled activations on hazardous inputs (RMU). That avoids gradient ascent's collapse, but the target behavior is defined only on the inputs you trained on.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Triage: hashes, magic bytes and strings
md: Strings lie by omission. Serious malware encrypts or encodes its strings and builds them at run time, so a short, clean strings list is not evidence of innocence. A file with almost no readable text at all is itself suspicious, as the packing lesson shows.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Packing, obfuscation and entropy
md: High entropy is a signal, not a verdict. Installers, compressed images in resources, and legitimately UPX-packed tools are high entropy too. Combine it with other signs: few imports, a writable and executable section, a raw size much smaller than the virtual size, or a section name that is not one of the usual ones.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Storage math: dimensions times bytes per number
md: Savings multiply, but so do quality losses. Each step (fewer dims, fewer bits) costs some recall, and the costs compound. Measure recall on your own queries at the exact size and precision you plan to serve, then use a rerank stage (next lesson) to win most of it back.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Distributed optimizer, MoE folding, overlap and measuring MFU
md: Every knob in this course trades three things: memory per GPU, communication on a specific link, and idle or redundant compute. MFU is the single number that tells you whether the trade worked.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Handles, mutexes, sockets and registry hives in memory
md: Every network row in memory names its owning process, and every handle names its holder. That pairing (this PID talked to that address, this PID opened that process) is what turns a list of artefacts into an attribution inside the host.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Size classes: buying speed with internal waste
md: `sizeof` is not what you pay. With a million 130-byte records you might budget 124 MiB, but jemalloc hands out 160 bytes each (153 MiB) and a power-of-two allocator 256 (244 MiB). Measure with `malloc_usable_size` or allocator stats, not by multiplying `sizeof`.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Acquire and release: publishing data across threads
md: Synchronization needs a pair on the same atomic: a Release (or stronger) write and an Acquire (or stronger) read that observes that write or its release sequence. Then everything before the write is visible after the read.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: RCU: publish a new version, free the old after a grace period
md: RCU protects readers from updaters, not updaters from each other. `rcu_assign_pointer()` does not make two concurrent updates safe; the example still takes `foo_mutex`. And a pointer from `rcu_dereference()` is valid only inside the critical section that fetched it.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Heap overflow: corrupting the neighbouring object
md: A heap overflow damages whoever happens to be next, and you cannot predict who that is: it depends on the allocator, the sizes and the order of allocations. Treat any heap overflow as able to corrupt any nearby object.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Triplet loss: the margin and easy, semi-hard, hard negatives
md: Hard is not the same as useful. The very hardest negatives in a large dataset are often mislabeled or badly imaged examples (FaceNet names both). Training only on them teaches the network to fit noise.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Warm caches in the benchmark, cold caches in production
md: A microbenchmark's working set and access pattern are part of the experiment. Report them next to the time, and sweep the size if the code's data can be large.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Token-in-token-out: train on the tokens you actually sampled
md: `role_content_only` is marked high risk. A tool-calling turn often has empty visible text, so two turns that called different tools can match. The stored prefix then wins, and the trainer keeps a history showing a call the agent never made, silently.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Learned indexes: a model that predicts where a key lives
md: Model execution must be nearly free. The paper's first attempt ran a 2-layer, 32-neuron net through TensorFlow from Python: about 80,000 ns per prediction, versus about 300 ns for a whole B-tree traversal. Their Learning Index Framework instead extracts the trained weights and generates small C++ index code, never calling TensorFlow at lookup time.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Static analysis: decompile, read the manifest, search the code
md: Misconception: "the URL is in the app, so it's fine to leave the bucket open: only our app knows it." Anything in the package is public (lesson 2). A storage URL, an API key or a hidden endpoint in an app is a published address.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Running a mobile app assessment end to end, and where to practise
md: A mobile assessment is three tests in one: the package (what anyone can read), the platform (what other apps and the device can reach) and the backend (what the server actually enforces). Most serious findings sit in the last two.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: MLA in production: kernels, prefill, parallelism, FP8 cache
md: MLA moves the cost of attention from memory to compute: one 576-wide row per token per layer, read by every head. That is a big win for decode, where memory traffic dominates, as long as you keep many heads on the GPU that holds the cache and use the non-absorbed form when compute dominates.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Why one phrasing of a question misses relevant documents
md: Retrieval quality depends on the exact words of the query. Multi-query retrieval treats the user's wording as one sample from many possible phrasings and retrieves with several samples instead of betting on one.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Bi-encoder, late interaction, cross-encoder: where the cost goes
md: Precompute versus interact. The more of the query-document comparison happens at query time, the more accurate and the more expensive the scorer. Bi-encoders and late interaction can serve as first stages over an index; cross-encoders only fit on short candidate lists.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Reusing the extra heads to decode faster
md: MTP gives two separate benefits: a training signal that can make the main model better, and heads that can draft tokens for exact, faster greedy decoding. You can use the first without the second by discarding the heads.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: SOAP: run Adam in the coordinates Shampoo discovers
md: SOAP = rotate into Shampoo's eigenbasis, run Adam there, rotate back. Refresh the rotation rarely; update Adam's statistics every step.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: What breaks in SP after a single training step
md: Random weights times activations grow like sqrt(n); updates times activations grow like n, because updates are correlated with the activations they act on. muP sets each layer's init and learning rate so that both effects stay order 1.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Transferring across depth: branch multipliers, Depth-muP, CompleteP
md: Width-only muP leaves the best LR drifting with depth. Scaling each residual branch by $L^{-\alpha}$, with AdamW block LRs scaled by $L^{\alpha-1}$, is the fix: Depth-muP's $\alpha = 1/2$ is one choice, but in CompleteP's pre-LN Transformer runs only $\alpha = 1$ kept the optimal HPs fixed across depth, and it keeps every layer learning features.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: Building a mutex on a futex: the three-state lock
md: A good futex mutex makes the uncontended path pure user space: one CAS to lock, one swap to unlock, zero system calls. The kernel is visited only when a thread really has to sleep, and unlock calls wake only if the word says someone might be sleeping.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Write skew: the bug that snapshot isolation lets through
